walkthroughs.body_html:
Organisms & Biodiversity — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Organisms & Biodiversity brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Organisms & Biodiversity.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Higher Simpson's diversity index D indicates:
options: Lower biodiversity
Higher biodiversity
No biodiversity
Same biodiversity

mcqs.q: Captive breeding is an example of:
options: In situ conservation
Ex situ conservation
Reforestation
Succession

mcqs.q: How are signals transmitted across a synapse between two neurones?
options: Via neurotransmitter chemicals released from the presynaptic neurone, which bind receptors on the postsynaptic neurone.
The electrical signal jumps directly from one neurone to the next across the synaptic gap.
Neurones touch each other at synapses and pass current through direct contact.
Phloem transports oxygen to all parts of the plant.

mcqs.q: What is transported in the phloem of a plant?
options: Phloem transports water from roots to leaves.
ADH directly opens holes in the collecting duct that let urine escape.
Sugars (mainly sucrose) and other organic compounds, from sources (e.g. leaves) to sinks (e.g. roots, fruits).
Phloem transports oxygen to all parts of the plant.

mcqs.q: How does ADH affect the collecting duct in the kidney?
options: ADH directly opens holes in the collecting duct that let urine escape.
It increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water (by inserting aquaporins), so more water is reabsorbed and urine is more concentrated.
Phloem transports oxygen to all parts of the plant.
ADH actively pumps water out of urine into the blood.
